name: netdom - Enumerate Domain Trusts
description: Enumerates domain trust relationships using the built-in Windows netdom tool. Shows trust direction (inbound/outbound/bidirectional), trust type (parent-child, forest, external), and which domains are trusted. Essential first step in trust-based attack chains — reveals paths to parent domains and foreign forests.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== UNDERSTANDING DOMAIN TRUSTS ===
Trusts define authentication relationships between domains/forests:
  Parent-child trust: automatic, bidirectional, transitive (within same forest)
    e.g., LOGISTICS.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL ↔ INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL
  Forest trust: between two separate forests (can be one-way or bidirectional)
    e.g., INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL ↔ FREIGHTLOGISTICS.LOCAL
  External trust: to a domain in another forest, non-transitive
  Shortcut trust: within forest, optimizes Kerberos paths

=== TRUST DIRECTION vs WHAT YOU CAN DO ===
  Inbound trust:  DOMAIN-A trusts DOMAIN-B = B users can auth to A's resources
  Outbound trust: DOMAIN-A trusts DOMAIN-C = A users can auth to C's resources
  Bidirectional:  both directions (most common for same-forest)

From attacker perspective:
  YOU ARE IN DOMAIN-B, domain-B has outbound trust to DOMAIN-A:
  → You can authenticate TO DOMAIN-A using domain-B credentials
  → You can kerberoast accounts IN DOMAIN-A with domain-B creds

=== POWERVIEW ALTERNATIVE ===
  Get-DomainTrust                      → trust info with more details
  Get-DomainTrustMapping               → recursive trust map
  Get-ForestDomain -Forest <fqdn>      → enumerate foreign forest domains
  ([System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()).GetAllTrustRelationships()

=== CHAIN POSITION ===
This is always the first card in trust-based attacks:
  1. Enumerate trusts (this card)
  2. Identify parent domain (child→parent ExtraSids attack) or forest trust
  3. Enumerate foreign forest for kerberoastable accounts or group members
  4. Escalate from child domain to parent (raiseChild.py or golden ticket ExtraSids)

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

recommended.note: Leverage trust data for cross-domain forging.

defense.why_it_works: netdom is a built-in Windows administrative tool that queries the domain's trustedDomain objects via LDAP. Any authenticated domain user can enumerate trust relationships — trust topology is stored in the domain NC and readable by all domain members by design. No privilege escalation is required.
defense.prerequisites: Any valid domain account. Domain-joined Windows host (or runas /netonly with domain credentials). netdom is installed by default on Windows Server; on workstations requires RSAT.
defense.impact: Reconnaissance output: trust directions (inbound/outbound/bidirectional), trust types (parent-child/forest/external), and trusted domain FQDNs. This is the attack-planning map — identifies paths to parent domains (child→parent ExtraSids attack) and foreign forests (cross-forest Kerberoasting). No immediate compromise, but critical for planning subsequent steps.
defense.detection: No dedicated event for trust enumeration via netdom. EDR process telemetry may flag netdom.exe execution on non-server workstations (rare in normal environments). LDAP query to trustedDomain objects in the domain NC is not individually logged but may appear in LDAP audit logs if enabled.
defense.prevention: Trust topology is readable by all domain members by design — cannot be restricted without breaking legitimate AD functionality. Prevention focuses on limiting who is domain-joined (zero-trust workstation policy) and detecting lateral movement that leads to the enumeration.
defense.evasion: netdom is a signed Microsoft binary (LOLBin) — does not trigger AV. Single command, minimal noise. Get-DomainTrust (PowerView) or native .NET API are alternatives that generate the same LDAP traffic without spawning netdom.exe.
defense.misconfiguration: Domain trusts (especially bidirectional and forest trusts) extend authentication boundaries. SID filtering is often disabled on forest trusts to support legacy applications — but this allows an attacker with Domain Admin in a child domain to forge a golden ticket with ExtraSids claiming Domain Admin SID in the parent/trusted forest. Without SID filtering (SIDHistory filtering), domain boundaries offer no security isolation.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Bidirectional forest trust without SID filtering:
Get-ADTrust -Filter * | Select-Object Name, Direction, SIDFilteringQuarantined
# SIDFilteringQuarantined: False  <-- SID filtering DISABLED
# Direction: BiDirectional        <-- both domains trust each other

# Child domain to parent: SID filtering is always disabled by default
# Enterprise Admin SID (S-1-5-21-<root>-519) can be added to ExtraSids
# Golden ticket with ExtraSids = cross-domain privilege escalation
defense.secure_config:
# Enable SID filtering on external/forest trusts:
netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes
# 'Quarantine' = SID filtering enabled — ExtraSids from other domain are stripped

# For child-to-parent trusts (SID filtering can't be enabled without breaking functionality):
# Use Selective Authentication instead of full trust
# Only accounts explicitly granted 'Allowed to Authenticate' can use the trust
netdom trust <ParentDomain> /domain:<ChildDomain> /SelectiveAuth:yes

# Restrict SIDHistory (prevents ExtraSids abuse):
# Audit accounts with SIDHistory:
Get-ADUser -Filter {SIDHistory -like '*'} -Properties SIDHistory

# Monitor cross-forest authentication:
# Event 4769 on parent DC with ticket from child domain user
